title: Why Does the Whole World Say "OK"?
parts: It may be the most used word on the planet, and the best-known story says it began as a joke about bad spelling.
You say it every day. At work, at home, in a text.
So what do the letters O and K actually stand for?
The best documented answer begins in Boston, almost two hundred years ago.
Most words point at something. Table. Run. Blue.
But OK points at nothing. It just says: yes, I agree, go on, I am listening.
A waiter asks if everything is OK. A friend says, OK, let's go. A mechanic says the car is OK. Same two letters, three different jobs.
Now travel back to Boston, in the late eighteen-thirties.
Newspaper writers there were playing a game. They would misspell a phrase on purpose, then shorten it to its initials.
No go became K.G., short for know go.
Small potatoes became S.P.
Another was O.W., short for oll wright, a silly spelling of all right.
Think of it as the text-message slang of its day.
Then, on March twenty-third, eighteen thirty-nine, the Boston Morning Post printed another one.
O.K. It stood for oll korrect, a joke spelling of all correct.
That is the earliest printed example that anyone has found.
It was dug up more than a century later, by a professor at Columbia University named Allen Walker Read.
He went through old newspapers by hand, and published what he found in the early nineteen-sixties.
But a joke in a newspaper rarely becomes a word that a whole country uses.
Many of those silly abbreviations vanished.
OK got lucky, because of an election.
In eighteen forty, President Martin Van Buren was running again. He came from Kinderhook, New York, and his nickname was Old Kinderhook.
His supporters shortened that to O.K. They put it on signs, formed OK Clubs, and used the slogan: Vote for OK.
Van Buren lost. But the two letters stayed.
His rivals even spread a made-up story that Andrew Jackson had invented OK by misspelling all correct. There is no evidence for it, but it kept people talking about the letters.
Now, a fair warning. This is the best documented explanation. It is not the only one.
Some people say OK comes from a Choctaw word, okeh. Others point to words from West Africa.
Scholars who looked for written evidence did not find a clear trail from those words to the American newspapers where OK first shows up.
Most modern dictionaries still go with Boston. But best explanation is not the same as case closed.
So why did OK survive, when its silly cousins disappeared?
It is tiny, easy to say, and easy to write.
And it is flexible. Yes, fine, understood: it fits into almost any sentence.
Allan Metcalf, who wrote a whole book about the word, says it even became a handy signal on the telegraph.
Today it is one of the most widely used terms in the world.
Think about that. A joke about spelling all correct wrong now lives on phones, and in conversations, all over the world.
It is almost two hundred years old, and you probably used it today without a second thought.
Here is another small thing you meet every day, and never question.
Pick up almost anything in a shop. The price ends in nine.
So why does everything cost nine ninety-nine, when we all know it really means ten?
